item.title: Canada Wildfires: What to Know
item.description:
As August begins, Canada’s wildfire crisis has shifted increasingly westward, where spreading flames have triggered evacuations and a provincial state of emergency in British Columbia weeks after smoke from Ontario fires choked cities to the south.

An explosive wildfire forced the evacuation of roughly 20,000 people from several Okanagan Lake communities on Saturday. The Bald Range fire was discovered around 5:30 p.m. Pacific time on Friday, about 10 miles northwest of Summerland, burning just 20 acres. Four hours later it had erupted to nearly 12,400 acres, said Erick Thompson, spokesman for the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen emergency operations. The fire is considered out of control.

“This being like a bomb going off,” British Columbia Premier David Eby said Saturday at a news conference. “A remarkable escalation of fire activity.”

About 12,000 residents of Summerland were ordered out shortly after midnight, followed by an additional 8,000 in nearby Peachland. Both communities sit on the lake’s western edge, about 240 miles east of Vancouver.

In July, nearly 200 wildfires burning in northwestern Ontario sent smoke across a large swath of Canada and the United States, fouling the air for millions and forcing hundreds of evacuations near the fire zones.

Rain and lower temperatures since then in many parts of the country helped Canadian firefighters bring hundreds of blazes under control, but days of darkened skies and unhealthy air raised tensions with the United States. A group of Republican lawmakers last month criticized Ottawa’s handling of the fires, and President Trump threatened to impose tariffs on Canada to pay for harm caused by the smoke.

Prime Minister Mark Carney did not directly respond to the complaints by Republican lawmakers, but he suggested the United States should do more to combat climate change, which scientists say is a significant factor in creating bigger, longer and fiercer wildfires.

As of Aug. 8, nearly 630 wildfires were burning across Canada, and have razed the most forest acres in the Northwest Territories, Ontario and Quebec.

On Saturday afternoon, 105 wildfires were burning in British Columbia, according to the B.C. Wildfire Service. Erratic winds, lightning storms and hot temperatures have stoked the blazes and more than 20,000 people had evacuated in the Okanagan region.

Videos posted on social media showed homes in Summerland in flames and fire burning on both sides of local roads. At least 55 people were airlifted to safety, Mr. Thompson said in a video broadcast. The province’s wildfire service has warned boaters to stay off Okanagan Lake, in the interior region, so as not to obstruct water bombers refilling their loads.

As of Aug. 8, 110 fires were burning in northwestern Ontario, down considerably from July, when the blazes spread aggressively across the remote, northwest part of the province, sending acrid smoke across several major cities. About a dozen rural and Indigenous communities were forced to evacuate.

The smoke darkened skies from northern Ontario to the East Coast of the United States, leaving New York, Toronto and Washington at times with the worst air quality in the world.

Roughly 9.5 million acres have burned in Canada, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Center.

The wildfire season in Canada typically runs from April to October, with August the last peak month.

Crews from Mexico have been dispatched to Canada to support hundreds of local firefighters, under an agreement between the countries, including the United States, to share fire resources in times of need.

About 100 Mexican firefighters arrived in British Columbia on Aug. 3, with another 200 landing a few days later. Ontario also received the help of 100 firefighters from Mexico,

Some evacuees in northwestern Ontario blamed local authorities for slow communication on the direction and danger of the fires. Officials, including Eleanor Olszewski, Canada’s minister of emergency management, have defended Canada’s forestry practices. “Warmer, drier weather is becoming more common, increasing wildfire risk in Canada and around the world,” Ms. Olszewski said in a statement in July.

Most wildfires in Canada spread across such vast, remote areas that they cannot be fought effectively and are often left to burn, experts say.

Half of Canada’s wildfires, like the blazes in northern Ontario, burn in sparsely populated areas, said Michael Flannigan, an expert on fire management at Thompson Rivers University in British Columbia. They are most often accessible only by plane.

Even if it were possible to to deploy firefighters to such remote areas, there is rarely enough time to react. Ignited mostly by lightning, wildfires often spread widely in the highly combustible boreal forest before firefighters can respond within the first critical 30 minutes.

In the long run, wildfires are considered beneficial because they remove the most flammable material in forests, promoting regeneration. Extinguishing every fire increases risk, as Canadian officials have learned in managing national parks.

Summer weather, like thunderstorms, can help clear smoke, but the smoke itself complicates the forecast. It can block sunlight, keeping temperatures lower at the surface and preventing storms from rising and intensifying.

As of early August, the smoke in Canada was concentrated in southern British Columbia and parts of northwestern Ontario.

Scientists estimate that wildfire smoke is linked to tens of thousands of deaths a year, and that human-caused climate change is responsible for a growing share of them.

item.title: ‘Out of Control’ Wildfire Forces Evacuation of 18,000 People in Canada
item.description:
A wildfire that is burning “out of control” in British Columbia, Canada, prompted an evacuation order of more than 18,000 people in two communities on Saturday as the blaze rapidly spread, the authorities said.

The Bald Range wildfire has scorched more than 23,000 acres as flames edged closer to the Districts of Summerland and Peachland.

The fire knocked out power in Summerland, which is about 260 miles east of Vancouver, officials said. The district declared a state of emergency on Saturday.

The District of Peachland, about 235 miles northeast of Vancouver, is known for its waterfront boardwalk along Okanagan Lake. Bottleneck Drive, a scenic network of rural roads connecting about 20 wineries, breweries and distilleries, is a well-known regional attraction in the District of Summerland.

The fire started on Friday around 5:30 p.m. local time, officials said. The cause of the fire is unknown.

Erick Thompson, a spokesman for the regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen’s Emergency Operations Center, said that anyone living in the District of Summerland, or other areas under the evacuation order, should leave their homes.

He called it “the most important thing you can do” in a video posted online of him leaving his home.

“Personal safety is the most important thing right now,” he said. “If this fire is near where you are, get what you need, make sure your family is safe, but you need to leave immediately.”

Conditions were not ideal for fighting the fire, Lisa Corcoran, a spokeswoman with the Central Okanagan Emergency Operations Center, told CBC in an interview on Saturday morning.

“It is hot, it is dry, it is windy, and we haven’t had rain in a long time,” Ms. Corcoran said. “Everything is just very, very dry out there.”

item.title: How a Drone ‘Hellscape’ Might Stop a Chinese Invasion of Taiwan
item.description:
To repel any future Chinese invasion, Taiwan is building fleets of flying drones and unmanned attack boats.

The goal is to use them to help locate and attack Chinese forces approaching the island, relying on Taiwanese soldiers trained to move quickly before China can strike them. U.S. commanders who developed this strategy call it a “hellscape”: overwhelming an invading force with waves of drones, missiles and artillery, and making an amphibious assault so risky that China’s leaders are deterred from trying.

Inspired by lessons from Ukraine and other recent war zones, Taiwan is now accelerating efforts to put that strategy into practice.

“Our drone and counter-drone efforts started relatively late, and initially we were trying things out as we went along,” Lt. Gen. Huang Wen-chi, the director general of strategic planning for the Taiwanese Defense Ministry, told a committee of lawmakers on Wednesday. That has begun to change over the past two years, he added.

On Thursday, Taiwan’s military allowed reporters to watch as troops in central Taiwan practiced using drones for reconnaissance, as part of the island’s annual Han Kuang military exercises, which began on Wednesday and will run for 10 days.

Maj. Gen. Lu Wen-yuan, who helped plan the exercises, said earlier that they would also train troops to take out enemy drones.

Many militaries across the world are embracing the drone revolution, but Taiwan faces a particularly urgent threat: China, which is roughly 110 miles away, claims the self-governed island as its territory. Chinese leaders say they want to absorb Taiwan peacefully, but will not rule out using force. They are backing that threat with expanding fleets of warships, planes, missiles and drones, as well as more frequent coast guard patrols and landing exercises.

Taiwanese officials have noted Ukraine’s drone-driven gains on the battlefield, and they are trying to emulate Ukraine’s David-versus-Goliath approach: using relatively cheap and nimble drones to level the playing field against a much larger adversary.

“Drones are entering a new chapter,” said Max Lo, the chairman of the Taiwan National Drone Industry Association. “Taiwan, for its own survival and national defense, is in urgent need of these drones. But it’s the same everywhere in the world right now — that’s an opportunity for Taiwan.”

Aiming to make the island a drone industry superpower, the government says it wants Taiwan to make 100,000 drones a month by 2030, with around half exported. It also wants the military to acquire over 210,000 flying and seaborne drones.

Taiwan has “realized that drones will be important in all the domains, in all the phases,” in a potential war with China, said Mick Ryan, a retired Australian major general who has studied Ukraine and Taiwan.

Ukraine’s recent success at longer-range drone strikes suggests that Taiwan could also attack ships leaving Chinese ports if Beijing launched an amphibious assault, said Mr. Ryan, now a senior fellow at the Lowy Institute in Sydney.

China’s army is not yet strong enough to easily invade Taiwan, many experts believe, and recent purges in the People’s Liberation Army’s high command have undermined its readiness. But like Taiwan’s military, it has been building up fleets of crewless planes and boats, and is investing heavily in technology to detect and jam drones.

“Remember, the Chinese are also watching everything the Ukrainians are doing,” Mr. Ryan added.

For Taiwan, acquiring the drones may be the straightforward part. To master drone warfare, Taiwan must also retool its military organization, training and doctrine. It must learn to operate swarms of drones, rapidly assess and share the intelligence they provide and prevent an enemy from disabling them, according to experts. This will require troops to be more mobile and self-sustaining.

“The army’s frontline military operations must undergo a total change from the past,” said Shu Hsiao-Huang, an associate research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research in Taipei, which is supported by Taiwan’s Defense Ministry. “In the Russia-Ukraine War, if you fire one round, you won’t have a chance to fire a second, if you just stay lined up there without moving on,” he said.

Unlike Ukraine, though, Taiwan lacks the pressure of an actual invasion to mobilize resources and force changes. “It’s very difficult, because they haven’t experienced the crucible of war,” Mr. Shu said.

But military units have been working to learn drone tactics, which are a focus of the continuing Han Kuang exercises.

The Taiwanese army also released pictures from a drill last month in which a unit scrambled to defend islands off Taiwan’s east coast by using drones to hunt for enemy forces. On Saturday, Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, watched an exercise in the island’s south where troops tested two types of prototype drones designed to strike invading forces.

Taiwan also recently created a Littoral Combat Command, integrating drones, mobile missiles and artillery into a coastal shield against potential Chinese invasion.

Still, Taiwan is a long way from meeting the complex demands of 21st-century warfare, many experts said. It risks becoming “focused on the technology more than the equally essential organizational and doctrinal changes that are needed to implement a hellscape concept,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security and an author of a recent study of Taiwan’s drone warfare strategy.

In the event of an invasion, China is likely to try to seal off Taiwan from external support. To survive a blockade, Taiwan needs to build stockpiles and expand homegrown drone production, especially “cheaper, shorter-range one-way attack drones,” Ms. Pettyjohn said.

Both sides of Taiwan’s polarized political landscape agree on building more drones, even if they disagree on the details. Taiwan’s government has proposed spending $6.5 billion over five years to buy drones. But two opposition parties that hold the majority in its legislature rejected the plan, arguing that it could attract graft and create waste. The main opposition Nationalist Party has proposed spending $7.4 billion over six years, with requirements for growing levels of domestic production.

As lawmakers debate spending, Taiwanese and U.S. drone makers are competing for potential orders.

Thunder Tiger, a Taiwanese manufacturer, and Shield AI, an American defense technology company, last month staged a trial run for two models of sea drones that could scout for enemy vessels and blow them up. But Chen Kwan-ju, the chairman of Thunder Tiger, said the company is seeking more policy certainty before it expands production partnerships.

At the same time, Taiwan is rapidly increasing its rate of drone exports, seeking to make itself an indispensable supplier of components for other democratic states that want to reduce their reliance on Chinese parts, which raise concerns about supply disruptions, or espionage.

In the first three months of 2026, Taiwan exported drones worth $115 million, exceeding its total drone exports for all of 2025, according to the island’s Ministry of Economic Affairs. The top destination is the Czech Republic, though many of the drones find their way to nearby Ukraine, research shows.

Taiwan’s exports of drone components are probably even higher. Demand for these parts, such as motors and optical equipment, is likely to grow, according to representatives of U.S. drone companies.

“Taiwan sits at the center of one of the most important industrial and strategic competitions of our time,” Michael Robbins, the president of the Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International, wrote in an email. “It is one of the few places positioned to produce trusted drone components at scale.”

item.title: Whirling for 7 Days and Nights, in Search of Ecstasy
item.description:
An elder gave a blessing, more than 100 people in a large hall recited Quranic verses and a musician played a melody on a reed flute, soon joined by about 15 bandmates on folk instruments and drums.

A woman in white took to the floor and began to spin, her skirt billowing as she accelerated and lifted her arms toward the sky.

Then came a man with a blond ponytail, a guy with a backward baseball cap, women in flowing dresses — all whirling.

This was the start of a recent gathering in southwestern Turkey focused on the ancient tradition of sema, the spinning form of prayer made famous by the so-called whirling dervishes.

Sema is rooted in the mystical Islamic tradition of Sufism and associated with the Islamic scholar and poet Jalaluddin Muhammad Rumi, who lived in what is now Turkey more than seven centuries ago.

In its best-known iteration, sema is performed by men, accompanied by male musicians, in choreographed ceremonies. In Turkey, it is often done for tourists who buy tickets.

This event, however, was open to everyone and led by a younger generation of whirlers who are making the ancient tradition their own.

The participants came from Turkey, France, Italy, Bulgaria, Iran, the United States and elsewhere. Many saw sema as part of a big-tent spirituality that encompassed Buddhism, yoga, astrology, shamanism and other traditions.

Instead of the classic white outfits and tall wool caps of the dervishes, they spun in embroidered shirts, baggy dresses, jeans, T-shirts and polka-dot socks.

Men whirled alongside women, with the women often outnumbering the men. The band at the heart of the gathering, Tumata, has both and is led by two sisters.

The event was organized to ensure that the whirling would continue nonstop for seven days and nights, with no fewer than two people spinning at any given time.

When I asked Cem Aydogdu, a Sufi guide in attendance, if there were any prerequisites for joining, he answered mystically.

“Whoever comes is called,” he said. “So whoever comes should be here. That’s including you.”

As for the purpose of a week of perpetual whirling, he said it created a vortex, like a whirlpool or tornado, that drew in energy to be dispersed.

“It’s not up to us where the energy goes,” said Mr. Aydogdu, 69, whose followers call him Cem Baba, or “Father Cem” in Turkish. “The one who is causing this to be generated knows where it’s supposed to go.”

The meeting took place at a retreat center with rustic accommodations surrounded by pine forests. It felt like a folk festival combined with a hippyish spiritual retreat.

There were a few rules. No drugs or alcohol, and no exposed backs, chests, bellies or legs in public areas. Rooms, bungalows and glamping facilities were available, but most people pitched their own tents. Attendance was free, but participants were expected to contribute to running costs and to volunteer, including helping with the three communal vegetarian meals per day.

Journalists from The New York Times joined for three days, which included a few hours of washing dishes and chopping onions, beets and leeks.

During the days, there were spiritual talks under a willow tree and whirling workshops for beginners. (Start slowly. Keep your vision blurry. If you feel sick, slow down!)

One afternoon, musicians played and people whirled at the opening of an outdoor market, recalling a story in which Rumi spontaneously spun to the sounds of jewelers hammering in a bazaar.

The gathering’s focus was the whirling hall: a stone-walled room where musicians took turns around the clock. Sometimes, only a few people whirled while others rested along the walls. Other times, two dozen whirlers filled the floor, spinning at different speeds, some with rhapsodic expressions, periodically calling out “Allah!” At one point, a young girl joined in, only to become dizzy and fall to the floor.

Sophie Fitzpatrick, 29, a chiropractor from Australia, said she initially felt awe and trepidation watching the experienced whirlers.

“I was scared of being the one who would fall over,” she said.

She eventually tried, felt nauseated and took a break, she said. The second time was easier and made her feel as if she was “part of something bigger.”

Sema has been practiced in Turkey for centuries and spread in the Ottoman Empire with the religious order founded by Rumi’s followers.

After the foundation of modern Turkey in 1923, its new, secular government shut down Sufi lodges and outlawed sema and other practices. Decades later, the government eased restrictions on the public performance of sema.

In 2008, the United Nations’ cultural agency recognized the sema ceremony as part of the “intangible cultural heritage of humanity.”

Melike Kilic, 25, an artist from Istanbul, said she had grown up with a strict version of Islam but was moved by the music and openness at her first sema gathering, which changed her view of religion.

“Allah turned into an entity that I can feel within, not this finger-wagging, scolding, judging figure,” she said.

Tumata, which was an organizer of the event, began in the 1970s. The band’s founder, the Sufi scholar and musicologist Rahmi Oruc Guvenc, organized sema gatherings lasting as long as 99 and 114 days. Since he died in 2017, his daughters have kept the band and the gatherings going.

One daughter, Kanikey Guvenc Akcay, 37, said the band sought to preserve the spirit of how it believed Rumi practiced sema — not focused on rules or choreography but on “ecstasy” and “the call of the heart.”

The event’s communal format hit a few snags. The organizers frequently reiterated the dress code (no shorts, beware of translucent pants), said they were short of volunteers and made it known that the donations were not keeping up with the size of the crowd. When only two whirlers remained on the floor, organizers walked through the outdoor dining area, calling for more.

But the sema never ceased, concluding late on the seventh day.

Many participants said they found the experience transformative.

Ilgaz Yuksel, from Istanbul, said he had left his job as a data scientist after living in a tent on a mountain during the coronavirus pandemic. He traveled to India, studied yoga and went to Thailand and Nepal. He took a vegan cooking course and now works as a chef in a plant-based restaurant.

While in India, he saw Rumi books and realized that he knew little about him, despite the poet’s having lived in Turkey. So he investigated Sufism and learned to whirl, finding it to be “a very powerful practice.”

“After an hour, you see your body start to whirl itself and you become the observer,” Mr. Yuksel, 33, said. “There is a kind of unity, oneness and peace.”

Elena Bogoslovova, 59, came from Bulgaria for the gathering and said she had discovered Sufism after being a drug addict and surviving a near-death experience. She found Tumata on YouTube and came to Turkey for one of its gatherings.

In the 17 years since, she has participated in many such events, she said, drawn by the teachings of love and acceptance and the feeling that “the spiritual traditions are real, not some Western retreat where you pay some money.”

She didn’t like to talk about sema, she said, because it was something you had to experience.

“You can see it and know about it, but to know it for yourself is different,” she said. “Otherwise it’s just crazy people whirling.”
